title: How She Sits Alone
sum: The book opens with a cry, 'eikhah, "How!", and a picture: Jerusalem as a woman sitting alone, a widow with no one to comfort her. For eleven verses a narrator describes the ruined city, with her roads empty, her priests groaning and her people searching for bread. Then, at verse 12, the city speaks for herself: "Does this not concern you, you travelers on the road?" She tells of fire in her bones, a net for her feet, a yoke woven from her own rebellions, and a winepress trodden on her young. She admits the LORD is right, and she asks him to look.

Everything that follows in the book is already here: the grief told as a woman's, the LORD named as the one who did it, the refrain "no one to comfort her", the confession of guilt beside the cry that the pain is too great, and a prayer that the enemies be made to feel what she feels. The chapter is an alphabet poem, one letter to a verse (below).
readings: Read as an eyewitness lament
The poem was composed within a few years of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC by someone who had seen it. The woman's voice is the poet's way of saying what a whole people felt.
Read as a city lament

Lamentations belongs to a very old family of songs written for destroyed cities in Mesopotamia, in which the city, personified as a woman, weeps. Israel's poet kept the form and changed what it says: the god is not absent or defeated; the LORD himself did it.
Read as liturgy
The poem was meant to be said aloud at a gathering of mourners, for example at the ruins of the temple (Jeremiah 41:5; Zechariah 7:3-5), and later every year on the Ninth of Av.

views.H: The siege began in the tenth month of King Zedekiah's ninth year; the wall was broken in the fourth month of his eleventh year; the temple was burned in the fifth month (2 Kings 25:1-9; Jeremiah 52:4-13). The Plain English Translation dates the fall to 586 BC; some scholars date it 587 BC. The chapter names real facts: the empty roads at festival time (1:4), the allies who failed (1:2, 19), foreigners walking into the temple (1:10), the famine (1:11, 19), and the captives (1:5, 18). Exiles had also been taken in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:14).
views.C: The Hebrew has no speaker labels; a narrator speaks of Zion in 1:1-11 and Zion speaks in 1:12-22, with a break in 1:9c and 1:11c where "I" cuts in. Some read this as two poets, others as one poet moving between voices (Berlin; Lee on the singers). 4Q111 has a different text at 1:7, 1:12, 1:14, 1:16 and 1:17-18 (see the variants), and 3Q3 preserves 1:10-12. The Greek and Latin Bibles have a prose preface that is not in the Hebrew.
views.J: The book is read on the Ninth of Av (Tish'ah be-Av), the day the rabbis mark for the fall of both temples, in a low voice, often sitting on the floor in a dimmed synagogue. Mishnah Ta'anit 4:6 lists five disasters of that day. Lamentations Rabbah opens with long introductions that retell the fall. The Talmud says Jeremiah wrote the book (Bava Batra 15a).
views.X: In the Roman Catholic Office of Tenebrae the lessons of the last days of Holy Week are taken from Lamentations, and the Hebrew letter names ("Aleph", "Beth") are sung before each verse. Composers such as Palestrina, Lassus, Tallis, Victoria and Couperin set them. Verse 12 is heard in Holy Week as Christ's voice from the cross (the Latin "O vos omnes"). The preface in the Greek and Latin Bibles and Jerome's attribution made Jeremiah the weeping prophet of the church too.
views.L: The chapter holds two things together that many readers separate: the city says "I defied his command" (1:18) and also "see my pain" (1:12) and "no one comforts me" (1:21). Dobbs-Allsopp, O'Connor and others point out that a book written in a woman's voice speaks of her shame (1:8-10), and that readers need care not to turn her pain into proof of her guilt. Survivors of war and abuse have found their own testimony in verses 12-22.

deep.b: This book's Plain English Translation is made from the Leningrad Codex word by word. The witnesses read for the variants are: the Qumran scrolls 3Q3, 4Q111, 5Q6 and 5Q7 in the Abegg, Bowley and Cook transcription; Swete's printed text of the Septuagint (mostly Codex Vaticanus), not the critical text of Rahlfs or Göttingen; the text of Jerome's Vulgate; and Rashi on Lamentations 4:20 and the Talmud (Ta'anit 22b) as read on Sefaria. The Targum and the Peshitta are not used as witnesses. In Swete's print Codex Vaticanus has no text at 3:22-24 and 3:29. The scrolls are small fragments, and in the transcription many words are restored, so only readings marked as visible are used and a restored word is never called a scroll's reading: 4Q111 preserves 1:1-18 and 2:5; 3Q3 preserves 1:10-12 and 3:52-62; 5Q6 preserves 4:5-8, 4:11-22 and 5:1-13, 16-18; 5Q7 preserves 4:17-20. The published editions are Baillet, Milik and de Vaux for 3Q3, 5Q6 and 5Q7 (Discoveries in the Judaean Desert III, 1962), and Cross for 4QLam (Discoveries in the Judaean Desert XVI).

The Greek Bible opens the book with a prose sentence that is not in the Hebrew: "And it happened, after Israel was taken captive and Jerusalem laid waste, that Jeremiah sat weeping and lamented this lament over Jerusalem, and said..." (translated here from Swete's text). The Clementine Vulgate has the same preface before the first letter, ending "...sighing and wailing in bitterness of spirit, he said". It is the earliest sign that Jeremiah was thought to be the speaker. The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew only, and does not add it.

Each verse starts with the next letter. Here ayin comes before pe (1:16-17), the usual order. In chapters 2, 3 and 4 pe comes first.

echoes: 2 Kings 25:1-21; Jeremiah 52:4-16; Deuteronomy 28:49-57; Isaiah 1:21; Isaiah 40:1; Psalm 79:1; Psalm 137:1; Jeremiah 8:18

settings.by: The poet, whom the Hebrew does not name (Jeremiah, by tradition)
settings.to: The survivors of Jerusalem and Judah, gathered to mourn; later the exiles in Babylon, and later still every Jewish community on the Ninth of Av
settings.when: After the fall in 586 BC, in the first years after the destruction; the temple site was still a place of mourning (Jeremiah 41:5)
settings.why: To say out loud what had happened and to name it as grief, not blame: a city that was crowded is alone, a princess is a laborer, and no one comforts her. The poet speaks of her in the third person so that listeners can stand beside her. Knowing this, the refrain "no one to comfort her" is a charge against the nations that were once friends, and also an invitation to the listeners to be the comforters.
settings.readers: The exiles, hearing it far from the ruins, learn that their loss was shared and was told in the right words; the Jews who read it every Ninth of Av are asked to mourn the fall of Jerusalem as though they were there.
views: Jeremiah 41:5 shows eighty men from Shechem, Shiloh and Samaria bringing offerings to the house of the LORD after the fall, and Zechariah 7:3-5 and 8:19 speak of fasts kept in the fifth month for seventy years. The poems fit that setting, where mourners gathered at the burned temple.
A minority view: the poems were composed or sent among the exiles, who needed a way to speak of the loss.
Dobbs-Allsopp and others see in the poems the Judean version of the Mesopotamian city lament, sung at a destroyed or rebuilt temple.

Jeremiah 9:17-20 calls for the mourning women to teach their daughters a lament, and 2 Chronicles 35:25 names singers who spoke of Josiah in laments. These may have performed the poems; the evidence is suggestive, not firm.

settings.by: Daughter Zion, the city as a woman
settings.to: First the passers-by on the road, then the LORD, then "all you peoples"
settings.when: The same time as the first part: the city speaks of the siege and the exile as things still raw
settings.why: To make the passers-by (and the listeners) look at her: this is the person to whom this happened. She asks God to see (1:20), admits her wrong (1:18) and asks for the same to be done to her enemies (1:21-22). The change of voice makes the sufferer, not an observer, the speaker.
settings.readers: For the first listeners, Zion's voice is a model of how to pray when God is the one who has done it: honest about guilt, honest about pain, and still addressed to him. For later readers (Christians in Holy Week, Jews on the Ninth of Av) it became a voice into which any sufferer could step.
views: The simplest reading: the personified city. Her 'young women and young men' (1:18) are her people.
Some think the 'I' of 1:9, 11 and 12-22 is the poet in a woman's voice, as in the funeral song of 2 Samuel 1.

title: The Lord Has Become Like an Enemy
sum: Chapter 2 is the hardest chapter of the book to read. For ten verses the verbs have one subject, the Lord: he has covered Zion with a cloud, swallowed her homes, cut off her horn, strung his bow like an enemy, torn down his own booth, spurned king and priest. The enemy appears only in passing. The temple the people loved is not defended but taken apart by the one who dwelt in it.

Then the poet turns (2:11) to his own tears and to the starving children, scolds the prophets who gave empty visions (2:14), and the passers-by who clap their hands. He tells the city to cry out in the night, and in the last three verses the city does, asking the LORD to look at what he has done: women eating their children, priest and prophet dying in the sanctuary, the young lying in the streets.
readings: Read as the covenant curses carried out
The chapter is the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 coming true, and 2:17 says so: the LORD "finished his word".
Read as protest
A poet who accuses God of acting like an enemy is arguing with him; the chapter never says that the punishment was fair in measure, only that the LORD did it.
Read as a record of trauma
The vivid pictures are what survivors saw, said as plainly as grief allows.

views.H: The chapter follows the last stages of the siege and capture: the breaking of the walls (2:8-9), the burning of the palaces and temple (2:5-7; 2 Kings 25:9), the capture of the king and princes (2:2, 9), the hunger (2:11-12, 19-20), the deaths of priests (2:20; 2 Kings 25:18-21). Its picture of mothers eating children matches the covenant curses (Deuteronomy 28:53-57) and the single story in 2 Kings 6:28-29.
views.C: The chapter's nearly unbroken chain of "he has" verbs is unlike the other chapters. Dobbs-Allsopp points out its likeness to the Mesopotamian laments, in which the gods hand the city to its destroyers. The Greek gives different readings at 2:1, 2:6, 2:13 and 2:14 (see the variants). Verse 18 has no clear subject.
views.J: Rabbinic tradition pictures God himself grieving over the destroyed temple (Bavli Berakhot 3a), and Lamentations Rabbah gathers many such stories. The chapter is read on the Ninth of Av.
views.X: Tenebrae lessons draw on Lamentations 2 for Good Friday. Calvin's lectures on Lamentations treat the chapter as showing that God does not spare his own people when they sin.
views.L: The chapter says what the pious usually do not: that God has acted as an enemy (2:4, 5). It does not smooth this over. Linafelt and Dobbs-Allsopp point out that the poem puts the blame on God's anger, not on the people, for ten verses, and that this was left in the Bible. The mothers and the children (2:11-12, 19-22) are the voice of those who have no part in the guilt the prophets name.

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:15-68; Leviticus 26:14-39; 2 Kings 25:9; Psalm 74:1-11; Psalm 79; Jeremiah 8:18-9:3; Ezekiel 24:16; Isaiah 63:10

settings.by: The poet, in the third person
settings.to: The community of survivors, and the LORD himself overhearing
settings.when: Soon after the fall, when the temple was a ruin
settings.why: To say what the people could hardly say: that the one who had been their defender had done it. The long list of verbs does not argue; it enumerates, so the hearers cannot look away. Knowing that the chapter was first heard by people who had believed in an inviolable Zion (Psalm 46; 48) shows how much it cost to say it.
settings.readers: The exiles and later readers meet a text that does not hurry to comfort; the later Ninth of Av reader is asked to stay with the loss before turning to hope.

settings.what: The poet's tears, and a call to cry out
settings.by: The poet, speaking to Daughter Zion
settings.to: The city personified, then her survivors
settings.when: The same days, with the famine at its worst
settings.why: To move from describing to addressing her: the poet says he cannot compare her to anything or heal her, scolds the prophets who did not warn her (2:14), mocks the mockers (2:15-16), and tells her to pray at night (2:18-19). The purpose is to start the prayer that 2:20 will say.
settings.readers: Teachers and priests of the later community are told how not to speak (false visions) and survivors are told to pray, with their hands raised, for their children.
views: The 'my eyes' of 2:11 and 3:48 sound like one speaker; this is a main reason the tradition thought of Jeremiah.
The voice may be that of a mourner trained to lead the people's weeping.

settings.when: In the night prayer the poet has just called for
settings.why: To make God look at what he has done: the children, the priests, the dead in the streets. The question 'whom have you ever treated like this?' is a complaint and an argument that no justice could account for this. The prayer asks for no answer and gets none in this chapter.
settings.readers: For the first hearers, the prayer was permission to complain to God in the language of the covenant, which was their only way to claim anything from him.

title: The Man Who Has Seen Affliction
sum: The middle of the book is a different poem. A single man says "I am the man who has seen affliction" and tells, in nearly twenty verses, how God has walled him in, turned into a bear and a lion, shot him through the kidneys and fed him wormwood. Then at verse 21 he says, "This I bring back to my heart", and the chapter turns. The LORD's acts of loyal love have not ended; his compassions are new each morning; the LORD is my portion; it is good to wait in silence. The next stanzas are about patience, the yoke, the cheek, and a God who does not afflict "from his heart".

The "I" then becomes "we" (3:40-47), the community confesses and accuses, and in the last stanzas the man speaks again, remembering a pit and a voice that said "Do not be afraid" (3:57), and ends with a prayer that his enemies be repaid. This is the one chapter built three verses to a letter (below).
readings: Read as the sufferer's journey
The man moves from complaint to hope to confession and back to prayer, and the chapter is the pattern of someone who lives with great pain.
Read as the book's center of faith
The famous verses 3:22-33 say what the rest of the book hopes for. The first 21 verses and last 20 say what that hope costs.
Read as an inserted psalm
Some think the chapter was written separately, as an individual lament psalm (Westermann), and set into the book by a later editor.

views.H: If the man is a particular person, the likeliest candidates are a king (Zedekiah in bronze chains, 2 Kings 25:7 and Lamentations 3:7; a king's loss, Lamentations 4:20) or a survivor. The chapter has no clear date marker. The pit of 3:53-55 recalls the cistern into which Jeremiah was lowered (Jeremiah 38:6), but the poem gives no date.
views.C: Chapter 3 differs from the others in form (three verses to each letter), voice (an individual, then a group, then the individual), and tone. Many scholars (Westermann among them) treat it as the work of a second poet or as an older poem. Others (Berlin; Dobbs-Allsopp) see it as part of the whole design. The Job parallels are close (Job 16:9-14; 19:7-12). The Hebrew has several uncertain places (3:22, 3:33, 3:34-36, 3:65). 3Q3 preserves 3:52-62.
views.J: Jewish readers have taken 3:25-30 as teaching about accepting God's discipline, and 3:22-23 as a statement of faith; Lamentations Rabbah comments at length on these verses. Bava Batra 15a makes Jeremiah the author.
views.X: Tenebrae and the Holy Saturday lessons of the old Roman Office use chapter 3. The man has been read as Christ (Matthew 5:39 beside Lamentations 3:30; Matthew 27:34 beside Lamentations 3:15 and 3:19; Isaiah 53 beside Lamentations 3:52-54), as the suffering believer, or as Jeremiah as a type of Christ. Calvin took the speaker to be Jeremiah. The hymn "Great Is Thy Faithfulness" (Chisholm, 1923) takes its title from 3:23.
views.L: The first 20 verses are among the bleakest in the Bible: God as bear, lion and archer (3:10-13). The turn does not cancel them. Many readers who use the book for pain see in 3:19-24 not a quick comfort but an act of will: the man chooses what to bring to mind, and the hope is spoken from inside the pit.

The turn of the chapter is built on waiting. Yachal (3:21, 24, 26) means to wait with trust; qavah (3:25) means to wait with hope, as for a cord to be pulled tight; and dumam (3:26) means to wait in silence. Waiting here is something the man does after he has said all he has to say, not instead of saying it.

deep.title: A guess: why the chapter has 66 verses
deep.b: Sixty-six is three times twenty-two, and no other chapter has this shape. My own guess, not a published view: the poet used the form that the Psalms had used for law (Psalm 119, eight verses to a letter) and made it fit grief by tightening it, so that the man's pain is bound in a pattern even when God seems to have left. It overlaps with the general idea that the alphabet gave grief a frame.

The Leningrad Codex marks places where the written consonants (Ketiv) and the form read aloud (Qere) differ: 3:10, 3:20, 3:25, 3:32 and 3:39. They are spelling or small changes of form, and the Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The ones that touch the sense are in the notes (3:32, 3:39).

echoes: Job 16:9-14; Job 19:7-12; Psalm 88; Psalm 69; Psalm 137:8; Jeremiah 20:7-18; Isaiah 50:6; Isaiah 53:8; Exodus 34:6-7; Deuteronomy 32:35

traditions.q: Does God cause both good and evil? (3:33, 37-39)
views: God ordains everything that comes to pass, yet is not the author of sin and does not take away the freedom of creatures; chapter 3 is read as God's rule over affliction and good alike. Westminster Confession 3.1 and 5.4-5.5; Calvin, Institutes 1.17-18.

God is sovereign and also hidden. Luther taught that the God who is preached is not to be confused with the hidden God who does what he wills; evil is not caused by God's will but permitted; the faithful hold to the revealed word of promise. Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI; Luther, The Bondage of the Will.

God never causes the evil of sin but permits it and draws good from it; he may will the evil of punishment, as a just ruler (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, 49, 2). The Catechism says God is in no way the cause of moral evil (Catechism 311).

God has not decreed sin or any person's damnation; his foreknowledge does not cause what he foresees. Wesley rejected the doctrine that God has fixed all events as the cause of sin, and taught that God desires all to be saved.

God does not will evil but permits it; John of Damascus distinguishes God's first will, which wills only the good, from his consequent will, which allows what free creatures choose and turns it to good.

traditions.q: May Christians pray for God to repay their enemies? (3:64-66; also 1:21-22)
views: The Liturgy of the Hours omits Psalms 58, 83 and 109 and some other verses because their tone is hard to pray as Christians; the Catechism asks Christians to forgive enemies and to pray for them (Catechism 2844).
Calvin read the prayers for vengeance in the Psalms as spoken in zeal for God's cause and not in private hatred, as a pattern for the faithful who may pray that God's justice be done.

Because Christ taught love of enemies and Anabaptists refuse the sword (Schleitheim Articles, article 6), these cries are laid before God as lament and the matter is left with him; the believer does not claim or carry out vengeance.

settings.by: A man who says 'I' and whom the Hebrew does not name
settings.to: God, and anyone who will listen
settings.when: After the fall; the images of walls, chains, pit and bow match a siege or imprisonment
settings.why: To describe what it is to be the target of God's hostility, in one sentence after another with God as the subject of every verb. By telling it in the first person he turns the community's grief into one person's. Knowing that the man's verbs are all aimed at him explains why 3:1-21 reads like Job 16 and 19 and not like a funeral song.
settings.readers: Later sufferers have taken the voice as their own: the exile who cannot pray, the sick, the abused.
views: Tradition from the Greek preface and the Talmud, and Jeremiah 20:7-18 for a similar voice.
Zedekiah or Jehoiachin: bronze chains (3:7), 'the LORD's anointed' later (4:20).
A soldier or citizen who lived through the siege.
The 'I' becomes 'we' at 3:40; a corporate personality.
A Job-like figure; Westermann's individual lament.

settings.by: The same man, now teaching himself and others
settings.to: Himself first ('says my soul'), then the community as a teacher speaking to the young
settings.when: As the man 'brings back to his heart' what he knows of God
settings.why: To say what he still holds to when everything points the other way: God's loyal love and compassion do not run out, the LORD is enough, waiting and silence are good, and God does not afflict for pleasure. The wisdom about the yoke and the cheek (3:27-30) is advice for others and is a school of patience; the lines about justice and the Most High's mouth (3:34-39) answer the accusation of 3:1-18 with a harder claim.
settings.readers: For the first community, this was the stretch to learn and recite. It is also the passage that the Ninth of Av reader hears as promise and that Christian sermons draw on most.

settings.by: 'We', the whole people, probably led by the man
settings.when: As the poem moves from private to public prayer
settings.why: To make the confession a group act: examine our ways, return, lift hands, say 'we have rebelled', and accuse God of not forgiving (3:42-45). It is confession and complaint in one breath. The 'we' also lets every later congregation say it.
settings.readers: The community that sang this was practicing repentance and protest together; the answer to 'you have not forgiven' is delayed to 5:21.

settings.what: The man remembers rescue and asks for repayment
settings.when: In the same lament, now looking back at a pit and a voice
settings.why: To remind God, and himself, that he has been heard before (3:55-57), then to ask that the same justice fall on his enemies. The prayer for repayment is the end of the individual's part and a counterpart of 1:21-22.
settings.readers: For the exiles, whose enemies were close, the prayer was an honest thing to say to God; for later readers it raises the question of how to pray for justice without hatred (see the card).

title: The Gold Grows Dim
sum: Chapter 4 returns to the first poem's shape, one letter a verse and two short lines each, and to its voice, the poet speaking about the city. Its method is comparison: gold and clay jars (4:1-2), jackals and a cruel people (4:3), delicate children and ash heaps (4:4-5), those killed by the sword and those killed by hunger (4:9), Sodom and Jerusalem (4:6). The poem shows what the siege did to the rich, the children and the women.

At 4:12 it asks why it happened and says it was the sins of the prophets and priests. It describes the fall: blind leaders stained with blood, help that never came, the chase in the hills, and the capture of "the LORD's anointed" (4:20). It ends with two sentences of judgment: the cup will pass to Edom, and Zion's guilt is paid in full (4:21-22).
readings: Read as description
The poem lists the effects of famine with terrible exactness: the skin black as soot, dry as wood.
Read as accusation
The poem names those it holds responsible: the prophets and priests.
Read as hope within grief
The last verse says Zion's guilt is paid and she will not be exiled again.

views.H: The famine (4:4-5, 8-10), the failure of an ally (4:17; Jeremiah 37:5-11), the flight and capture of King Zedekiah at Jericho (4:18-20; 2 Kings 25:4-7) and the part played by Edom (4:21-22; Psalm 137:7; Obadiah 10-14) are all in the record. The belief in Zion's safety (4:12) fits the songs of Zion (Psalm 46; 48; 76) and Jeremiah 7:4.
views.C: The poem has the closest likeness to chapter 1, though it keeps a clinical distance. 5Q6 preserves 4:5-8 and 4:11-22; 5Q7 preserves 4:17-20. Textual notes: the jackals (4:3), the nobles (4:7), the unclean cry (4:15), the 'anointed' (4:20) and Uz (4:21). Some read 4:22 as a later hopeful addition; others as the poem's own ending.
views.J: Rabbinic readers took Edom to be Rome, and 4:21-22 as a promise that Rome would drink the cup. Rashi on 4:20 takes the anointed to be Josiah. Lamentations Rabbah retells the siege with many stories. The 'anointed' has also been read messianically.
views.X: Christian readers have taken 4:20 as a picture of Christ's arrest, helped by the Greek and Latin 'Christ the Lord'. Verse 13, on the sins of prophets and priests, is often read as a warning to church leaders.
views.L: The comparison of deaths (4:9) and the cooked children (4:10) are among the book's hardest lines; the Plain English Translation does not soften them and does not add to them. The poem puts the blame for the city's end on its leaders (4:13) as well as on the people's sin, a verse later readers have used to hold religious leaders to account.

deep.b:
Each verse starts with the next letter. Here pe comes before ayin (4:16-17), as in chapters 2 and 3.

The Leningrad Codex marks places where the written consonants (Ketiv) and the form read aloud (Qere) differ: 4:3, 4:12, 4:16, 4:17 and 4:21. They are spelling or small changes of form, and the Plain English Translation follows the Qere. The one that touches the sense (jackals or sea monsters) is in the note at 4:3.

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:53-57; Genesis 19; Ezekiel 16:48-50; Jeremiah 25:15-29; Jeremiah 49:7-22; Obadiah 10-16; Psalm 137:7; Ezekiel 19; 2 Kings 25:4-7; Psalm 89:38-51

settings.by: The poet, in the third person
settings.to: Those who knew the city before and after, the survivors
settings.when: Some time after the fall, with the famine still fresh
settings.why: To make the loss measurable by comparing what the city's people were with what they became. The comparisons of gold with clay, jackals with a cruel people and sword with hunger all do the same thing: they force the hearer to see the change. Knowing that the first listeners had seen it themselves makes these lines a testimony, not a description for strangers.
settings.readers: Later readers, who have not seen a siege, are asked to see what hunger does to the beautiful and the weak.

settings.what: Why it happened, and the fall
settings.to: The community, which had believed Zion would not fall
settings.when: Looking back on the last days of the siege
settings.why: To name a cause (the sins of prophets and priests), to show the hope that failed (a watchtower, a nation that does not save), and to mourn the captured king. The cause is given so that the people will not blame only the enemy; the king is named as the loss they cannot get over.
settings.readers: For the first community, the 'we' of 4:17-20 put each hearer among those who watched from the tower; for later Jewish and Christian readers, 4:20 became a place to think about kingship and the Messiah.
views: The commonest view: the king caught near Jericho (2 Kings 25:4-7).
Tradition (Rashi, the Chronicles verse 35:25) links the verse to Josiah, though Josiah died at Megiddo (2 Kings 23:29).
Christian readers have read 'the anointed' as Christ; this is a reading laid over the Hebrew.

settings.what: The cup for Edom, the end for Zion
settings.to: Daughter Edom, by apostrophe; and Daughter Zion
settings.when: As the poem's last word, looking forward
settings.why: To turn the ending: the judgment on Zion is complete, and Edom, who rejoiced, will drink the cup. The poet speaks to Edom ironically ("be glad") so that the survivors hear the warning and the promise at once.
settings.readers: The community hears a comfort at the end of the most bitter poem; later Jewish readers heard 'Edom' as whoever oppressed them.

title: Remember, LORD
sum: The last poem is a prayer from the community, in the first person plural. It has 22 verses, the number of letters in the alphabet, but it is not an acrostic. It does not describe a city as a woman; it says "we" and "our". It begins with three imperatives, "remember", "look" and "see", and then lists what has been lost: land, fathers, water, wood, safety, food, daughters, princes, elders, young men and music.

At 5:19 it turns: "You, LORD, sit as king forever." Then come the last questions. Why do you forget us? Bring us back to yourself and we will come back; make our days new. And then, unless you have rejected us altogether. The book stops there. In Jewish reading 5:21 is repeated so the book does not end on that note (see 5:21).
readings: Read as a prayer of the exiles
A communal petition, the kind sung at a fast, with the usual parts: a call to God, a list of troubles, a confession and an appeal.
Read as a broken alphabet
The poem has the length of an acrostic but not the letters. Some read this as the end of order: grief that finally gives up the form.
Read as an open ending
The book does not say God answers. It ends on a question.

views.H: The losses fit the years after 586 BC: land taken by outsiders (5:2; Ezekiel 35:10), the poor on Judah's land (Jeremiah 39:10), raids from the wilderness (5:9), foreign rulers (5:8), women raped (5:11), nobles hanged (5:12; 2 Kings 25:21), forced labor (5:13), the empty gate and the silent music (5:14-15) and the ruined Mount Zion (5:18). Egypt and Assyria (5:6) are the old allies and powers.
views.C: Chapter 5 differs in form from the others (22 verses but no alphabet, short lines of about three beats) and in voice (the whole community, not Zion or the man). Commentators think it is later than 1, 2 and 4, or that it was the final prayer added to the collection. 5Q6 preserves 5:1-13 and 16-18 and agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling; no scroll preserves 5:19-22. The Greek of Codex Vaticanus reads 5:13 differently and takes 5:22 as a statement.
views.J: The Masoretic practice, still followed in synagogues, repeats 5:21 after 5:22 so the book ends with the prayer for return.
views.X: The Roman Office of Tenebrae used 5:1-11 as the 'Prayer of Jeremiah' on Holy Saturday, ending with 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem, return to the LORD your God', which the Hebrew does not have. Christians have read 5:7 in light of original sin (see the card). These are readings laid over the poem.
views.L: The chapter names what survivors name: shame (5:1), hunger, poverty, loss of the young, and the violation of women (5:11), and ends with the hardest question, whether God has turned away for good. Linafelt reads the silence at the end as the point: the book lets grief stand without an answer. The confession in 5:16 beside the complaint of 5:20 is the same pairing as in chapter 1.

deep.b: Chapters 1 to 4 are alphabet poems. Chapter 5 has 22 verses, but each does not begin with a successive letter. Commentators discuss why: the number may be an echo of the alphabet, the poem may deliberately drop the pattern, or it may belong to a different stage of the collection. This page gives no table, because there is no pattern to show.

The Leningrad Codex marks places where the written consonants (Ketiv) and the form read aloud (Qere) differ: 5:1, 5:3, 5:5, 5:7 and 5:21. They are spelling or small changes of form, and the Plain English Translation follows the Qere. None of them changes the sense.

echoes: Isaiah 49:14-16; Isaiah 54:1-10; Jeremiah 31:18-19; Psalm 80:3; Psalm 102:12; Psalm 44; Exodus 20:5; Ezekiel 18:2; Hosea 14:2

traditions.q: Do children carry their parents' guilt? (5:7)
views: Original sin is passed on by generation. It is a state of the human race, "contracted" and not "committed", a deprivation of original holiness and justice, and not a personal fault of each child (Catechism 404-405).
Sin passes on as 'ancestral sin': mortality and a weakened will, but not guilt for Adam's act. Each person answers for his own sins.
Every person is born with original sin, which is truly sin and brings condemnation to those not born again (Augsburg Confession, article 2).
The guilt of Adam's first sin is counted to his descendants, and the corruption passes on (Westminster Confession 6.3; Heidelberg Catechism, questions 7 and 8).
Adam's fall gave his descendants a nature inclined to sin, and each, as soon as he can act morally, becomes a sinner under condemnation (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article 3).
People will be punished for their own sins and not for Adam's transgression (Articles of Faith, article 2).

settings.what: A prayer of remembrance and loss
settings.when: Some years after the fall: the land has new masters, and the effects of the siege are still felt (5:2-14)
settings.why: To place the whole record of loss before God and ask him to remember. The prayer does not argue; it enumerates, and names its own sin (5:7, 16) without making that the reason for silence. The list also serves as a memorial: what the people had, they lost.
settings.readers: The first community may have used the chapter as a prayer at a fast (a guess; the book does not say); later it became the end of the book read in synagogue and church.
views: The chapter has the form of a communal lament, as in Psalms 44, 74 and 79, and fits the fasts of Zechariah 7:3-5.
Some think it was composed among the exiles in Babylon, the 'we' of slaves who rule (5:8) and forced labor (5:13).

settings.when: At the close of the whole collection
settings.why: To set God's unending kingship against the people's long abandonment, to ask him to bring them back and renew their days, and to end with the question whether he has turned away for good. The 'unless' is a plea, and not a settled statement, because 5:21 has already asked.
settings.readers: Later Jewish readers repeated 5:21 so that the book does not end on the last words; Isaiah 49:14-16, where God answers Zion's complaint that he has forgotten her, is often read as the reply.
views: Unless you have utterly rejected us
The Masoretic reading (a conditional left unfinished), kept in the Plain English Translation.
The Greek and Latin: a statement.
